claims.statement: Alloy 625 is identified as UNS N06625 and W.Nr. 2.4856; NiCr22Mo9Nb is a common European designation.
claims.conditions: Confirm against the supplied material certificate and governing product specification.

claims.statement: The Special Metals bulletin lists limiting composition of Ni 58.0% minimum, Cr 20.0–23.0%, Mo 8.0–10.0%, Nb plus Ta 3.15–4.15%, Fe 5.0% maximum, and C 0.10% maximum, with additional limits for Mn, Si, P, S, Al, Ti, and Co.
claims.conditions: Weight-percent limits in the cited bulletin; product-specific chemistry and current specification control procurement.

claims.statement: Alloy 625 obtains its baseline strength from molybdenum and niobium stiffening of a nickel-chromium matrix, so precipitation-hardening treatment is not required for its principal strengthening mechanism.
claims.conditions: Cold work and product condition can substantially change strength.

claims.statement: Alloy 625 is described as a face-centered-cubic, solid-solution matrix-stiffened alloy and may contain MC and M6C carbides.
claims.conditions: Actual microstructure depends on melt, processing, heat treatment, and exposure.

claims.statement: The bulletin presents Alloy 625 service use from cryogenic temperatures to approximately 982°C, while its quick-reference material describes high strength from cryogenic temperatures to approximately 815°C; these are application and property-context statements, not universal design limits.
claims.conditions: Use the governing code, product form, exposure, stress, time, and design allowable for a real component.

claims.statement: The bulletin gives density of approximately 8.44 g/cm³ and a melting range of approximately 1290–1350°C; it also reports low magnetic permeability and temperature-dependent thermal properties.
claims.conditions: Typical published values; verify the relevant product and temperature range for analysis.

claims.statement: The high Ni-Cr-Mo alloy content provides broad aqueous-corrosion resistance, including strong resistance to localized attack such as pitting and crevice corrosion in many chloride environments.
claims.conditions: Resistance is not immunity; assess temperature, chlorides, deposits, crevices, oxidants, galvanic coupling, flow, surface, weld condition, and stress.

claims.statement: Alloy 625 is used in seawater-related applications because of resistance to localized corrosion, chloride-ion stress-corrosion cracking, high tensile strength, and corrosion-fatigue strength.
claims.conditions: Site-specific seawater, cathodic-protection, crevice, and fatigue assessment is still required.

claims.statement: Alloy 625 is reported to resist high-temperature oxidation and carburization in addition to aqueous corrosion mechanisms.
claims.conditions: Performance depends on gas chemistry, temperature, exposure time, thermal cycling, surface condition, and stress.

claims.statement: Alloy 625 can be joined by conventional welding processes; Alloy 625 filler metal and Welding Electrode 112 are described for joining Alloy 625 and selected dissimilar nickel, stainless, and corrosion-resistant alloys.
claims.conditions: Weld procedure qualification, cleanliness, shielding, heat input, dilution, joint design, and inspection remain necessary.

claims.statement: The cited bulletin states that the recommended Alloy 625 weld products do not require post-weld heat treatment to retain their high strength and ductility.
claims.conditions: This does not override a code-, procedure-, service-, or dissimilar-joint-specific thermal-treatment requirement.

claims.statement: Niobium-bearing Alloy 625 weld metal can develop microsegregation and secondary constituents during solidification; these can influence local corrosion and mechanical behavior, especially in weld overlays and additive or high-dilution deposits.
claims.conditions: Characterize the actual weld procedure and deposit rather than extrapolating from wrought base-metal data.

claims.statement: Published work demonstrates that Alloy 625 weld and friction-stir-processed conditions can have measurable differences in intergranular-corrosion susceptibility and degree of sensitization.
claims.conditions: Study-specific material, process, and ASTM G28 / DL-EPR testing; not a universal acceptance limit.

claims.statement: Nickel Institute guidance notes that as-welded Alloy 625 can have lower crevice-corrosion resistance than parent 6% Mo metal and may require a more highly alloyed consumable for certain seawater joints.
claims.conditions: Apply only after checking the joint, base metal, consumable, environment, and design basis.

claims.statement: Cold working can increase Alloy 625 tensile strength and hardness for moderate-temperature applications, but the resulting condition must be controlled because ductility, residual stress, forming history, and service temperature change with cold work.
claims.conditions: Do not substitute cold-worked values for the delivered certificate or code allowables.

claims.statement: Alloy 625 is described as fabricable, weldable, and brazeable, but it work-hardens and requires controlled machining practice, tooling, feeds, speeds, and heat removal.
claims.conditions: Process guidance is product- and equipment-specific.
claims.locator: pp. 1 and 14–15; fabrication and machining sections

claims.statement: Alloy 625 appears in multiple product-form standards and code contexts, including ASTM B443, ASTM B446, ASTM B564, and ASME material provisions; a UNS number alone does not define form, heat treatment, dimensions, testing, inspection, or allowable stress.
claims.conditions: Verify the current edition and exact product-form specification before procurement or design.

claims.statement: NACE MR0175 / ISO 15156 may be relevant to Alloy 625 sour-service selection, but compliance depends on exact alloy/product condition, hardness, heat treatment, environment, and applicable limits; the designation alone is not a qualification.
claims.conditions: Check the current controlled standard and apply it through a qualified materials review.
claims.locator: Applicable specifications section; verify current NACE/ISO requirements separately

claims.statement: Published applications include marine and seawater equipment, chemical-processing vessels and piping, aerospace ducting and exhaust systems, heat exchangers, pollution-control equipment, nuclear components, and oil-and-gas equipment.
claims.conditions: Application examples are not proof of fitness for a particular design or service environment.
